8689.m: The female is called a leopardess.

8698.q: How many official languages does the Confederation use for its official texts?
8698.e: The Confederation officially uses German, French and Italian as official languages. Romansh is only used in certain cases, even though it is a national language.
8698.m: The Confederation works in three official languages.

8730.q: What does the name “United Nations” mean?
a: Countries that have joined together to act together
Countries that have a shared king
Countries that all speak the same language
Countries that form a football team together
8730.e: The name shows that many states in the world have united to solve problems together. Almost all the countries in the world belong to it.
8730.m: United Nations means that countries work together.

8731.q: What does the International Monetary Fund (IMF) do?
a: It helps countries in financial crises with loans
8731.e: The IMF supports countries that have got into economic difficulties with loans and advice. Switzerland is also a member.
8731.m: The IMF helps countries that are short of money.

8738.q: When do brown trout normally spawn?
a: Only at full moon in July
8738.e: Unlike many other fish, the brown trout lays its eggs in autumn and winter. The young fish then hatch in winter or spring.
8738.m: Brown trout spawn in autumn and winter.

8755.q: What often happens when a dictator dies?
a: Often a family member takes over power.
The country immediately becomes a democracy.
There is no government any more.
8755.e: In some dictatorships, such as North Korea, power passes down in the family, for example from father to son. That way control stays in a few hands.
8755.m: Power often stays in the family.

8766.q: What does the ‘majority of the cantons’ mean in a vote?
a: Most of the cantons must agree
Only the Council of States decides
Every canton votes the same way as the people
8766.e: For changes to the constitution, as well as a majority of the voters, a majority of the cantons is needed too. This is called the majority of the cantons.
8766.m: For the majority of the cantons, most cantons must agree.

8772.q: Which group of vertebrates does the leopard belong to?
8772.e: Leopards have fur, give birth to live young and feed them with milk. These are typical features of mammals.

8777.q: What does blood do in your body?
a: It takes oxygen and food everywhere
8777.e: Blood flows through your whole body and brings oxygen and nutrients to the cells. With a small cut, a little of it comes out.

8797.q: Roughly how many vertebrae does the human spine have?
8797.e: The spine is made of several sections with about 33 vertebrae altogether. It supports the body and protects the spinal cord.

8806.q: Which sense organ do you need to see?
8806.e: With your eyes you take in light, colours and shapes. The brain then puts these pictures together.

8825.q: What is on the brown trout's menu?
8825.e: The brown trout eats animals such as insect larvae, freshwater shrimps, worms and small fish. It also snaps up insects that fall onto the water.
8825.m: It eats insects, crustaceans and small fish.

8852.q: What happens to a ray of light when it passes at an angle from air into water?
a: It is refracted and changes direction
8852.e: Because light is slower in water than in air, the ray bends as it passes from one to the other. This is called refraction.

8853.q: Which is the only country in the world with a triangular rather than rectangular national flag?
8853.e: Nepal is the only country in the world with an official national flag that is not rectangular. It consists of two triangles, one above the other.
8853.m: Nepal is the only country without a rectangular flag.

a: A group of military officers who have taken power.
8885.e: A junta usually consists of senior officers who rule together after a coup. It often shuts down democratic institutions.
8885.m: Military officers rule together as a junta.

8898.q: What does it mean that Switzerland is “neutral”?
a: It does not get involved in other countries’ wars
It has no government of its own
It is not allowed to vote
It does not belong to any continent
8898.e: Being neutral means that Switzerland does not take sides in wars between other countries. This has been the case for a very long time.
8898.m: Neutral means not taking sides in a war.

8915.q: In which year did women in Switzerland get the right to vote at federal level?
8915.e: Only in 1971 were Swiss women allowed to vote and elect at federal level for the first time. Compared with other countries, that was very late.
8915.m: Women have had the vote at federal level since 1971.

8940.q: What does the leopard in the picture like to eat most?
8940.e: The leopard is a meat-eater. It mainly catches medium-sized hoofed animals such as antelopes, but smaller animals too.

8943.q: Why can you see nothing at all in a completely dark room?
a: Because there is no light there
Because the air there is different
Because it is too quiet there
8943.e: We can only see things when light from them enters our eyes. Without light there is nothing for our eyes to catch.
8943.m: Without light we cannot see anything.

8947.q: What happens if you squeeze a metal spring and then let go?
8947.e: A spring stores force when it is squeezed. When you let go, it releases the force again and springs back.
8947.m: Springs store force and give it back.

a: A group of countries that share the French language
8956.e: La Francophonie links countries and regions where French is spoken, including French-speaking Switzerland. It promotes culture and cooperation.

8958.q: Which country is often called “Europe’s last dictatorship”?
8958.e: Belarus under Alexander Lukashenko is often called “Europe’s last dictatorship”. Elections there are not considered free and fair, and critics are persecuted.
8958.m: Belarus is seen as Europe’s last dictatorship.

9004.q: What is EFTA, which Switzerland also belongs to?
a: A free trade association of European states outside the EU
9004.e: EFTA (the European Free Trade Association) links countries such as Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, which do not belong to the EU but still want to make trade easier.
9004.m: EFTA promotes free trade outside the EU.

9026.q: How many golden stars are on the flag of the European Union?
9026.e: The EU flag shows twelve golden stars in a circle on a blue background, regardless of the number of member states. Twelve stands for completeness and unity.
9026.m: The EU flag always has 12 stars.

9029.q: What was the well-known small car from East Germany called?
9029.e: The Trabant was a simple car built in East Germany. Many people had to wait a long time to get one.
9029.m: The Trabant was the car of East Germany.

9036.q: Why are bogs important for the climate?
a: They store large amounts of carbon in the ground
They make oxygen faster than forests
They cool the Earth strongly through evaporation
They stop rain in the surrounding area
9036.e: Bogs are made of dead plant remains that hardly break down under water. As a result a lot of carbon stays locked in the ground instead of entering the air as CO2.
9036.m: Bogs store a lot of carbon in the ground.

9043.q: What does electrical resistance in ohms tell you?
a: How much a material hinders the flow of electricity
How much light a material lets through
9043.e: A high resistance means that a material strongly hinders the flow of electricity; a low resistance lets electricity flow easily. Metals such as copper have a very low resistance and therefore conduct well.
9043.m: Resistance slows down the flow of electricity.

9051.q: What is the capital of Switzerland?
9051.e: Switzerland's government and parliament work in Bern. Many important decisions are made there.
9051.m: Bern is the capital of Switzerland.

9078.q: What do you have fingernails for?
9078.e: Nails are made of a hard material called keratin. They protect the sensitive skin at the fingertips.

9083.q: What does the presence of brown trout tell you about a stream?
a: The water is clean and rich in oxygen
The water is full of mud
9083.e: The brown trout needs very good water quality. That is why it shows that a stream is healthy.
9083.m: Trout are a sign of clean water.

9105.q: Who was an important communist leader in Vietnam?
9105.e: Ho Chi Minh fought for an independent, communist Vietnam. The city of Saigon was later named after him.
9105.m: Ho Chi Minh led the communists in Vietnam.

9106.q: Which country has a red and blue Taegeuk symbol, similar to yin and yang, in the centre of its flag?
9106.e: The South Korean flag shows the red and blue Taegeuk symbol in the middle, which stands for harmony. Four black trigrams are arranged around it.
9106.m: South Korea shows the Taegeuk symbol.

9143.q: Which vitamin does your body make in the skin with the help of sunlight?
9143.e: When sunlight falls on the skin, the body makes vitamin D. It is important for strong bones.

9168.q: Who composed the famous song “The Trout” (“Die Forelle”)?
9168.e: In 1817 Franz Schubert set to music a poem about a trout in a stream. Later he also wrote the “Trout Quintet”.

a: A group that collects signatures to put a law to the people
A committee of the Federal Council
A department of the Federal Chancellery
9220.e: If citizens do not agree with a new law, they can join together in a referendum committee. They then collect signatures for the optional referendum.
9220.m: Referendum committees collect signatures against laws.

a: China’s communist dictator, responsible for millions of deaths.
9236.e: Mao Zedong ruled China from 1949 to 1976. Programmes such as the “Great Leap Forward” and the “Cultural Revolution” cost millions of people their lives.
9236.m: Mao ruled China with a harsh hand.

9243.q: Why does a metal handle feel colder than a wooden handle, even though both are the same temperature?
a: Metal conducts heat away from your hand faster
Metal is always really colder than wood
Your skin is allergic to metal
9243.e: Metal is a good conductor of heat and draws the heat away from your hand quickly. Wood conducts heat badly, so it feels warmer, even though both objects are the same temperature.
9243.m: Good conductors of heat feel colder.

9254.q: Which animal family does the leopard in the picture belong to?
9254.e: The leopard is a predator from the cat family. Within it, it counts as one of the big cats.
9254.m: The leopard is a big cat.

9256.q: What does the Federal Council do?
9256.e: The Federal Council is made up of several people who run Switzerland together. They make important decisions for the whole country.

9260.q: Why do astronauts wear a special suit in space?
a: Because there is no air to breathe there
Because it always rains in space
Because it is very loud there
Because there is a lot of dust there
9260.e: In space there is no air and no oxygen. The spacesuit gives the astronauts air and protects them from cold and heat.
9260.m: In space there is no air to breathe.

9263.q: What is particularly harmful to brown trout in a stream?
a: Sewage and fertiliser, which use up oxygen
9263.e: Polluted water often contains less oxygen and also toxic substances. Trout cannot cope with that well.

9264.q: You rub a balloon on your jumper and hold it against the wall. What happens?
a: The balloon sticks to the wall
The balloon falls straight to the floor
9264.e: Rubbing gives the balloon an electric charge. This static electricity pulls it to the wall.
9264.m: Rubbing gives things an electric charge.

9268.q: What decides which blood group (A, B, AB or 0) a person has?
a: Certain markers on the surface of the red blood cells
9268.e: Certain proteins sit on red blood cells. Their combination decides the blood group.
9268.m: Blood groups come from proteins in the blood.

9287.q: What role does the pancreas play in the digestive system?
a: It produces digestive enzymes and hormones such as insulin
It stores fat for the winter
It filters the air you breathe
9287.e: The pancreas releases enzymes into the gut that break down food. It also produces hormones such as insulin, which control blood sugar.
9287.m: The pancreas helps with digestion and blood sugar.

9318.q: What is the old town of Solothurn especially known for?
a: Its many old churches and towers
9318.e: Solothurn has a beautiful old town with many old churches, towers and fountains. That is why many tourists like to stroll through its narrow lanes.
9318.m: Solothurn's old town has many churches and towers.

9322.q: Which greenhouse gas is produced, among other things, by keeping livestock and has a particularly strong effect on the climate?
9322.e: Methane is produced, for example, when cows digest their food. Over a short time it affects the climate even more strongly than CO2.
9322.m: Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas.

9335.q: What was the ‘Ostpolitik’ of German Chancellor Willy Brandt?
a: A policy of West Germany drawing closer to East Germany and the Eastern Bloc
A plan to build the Berlin Wall
A military alliance against the Soviet Union
An economic blockade against Eastern Europe
9335.e: From 1969 Willy Brandt sought dialogue with East Germany and other communist states. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for this in 1971.
9335.m: Ostpolitik meant drawing closer to the East.

9347.q: How can experts tell the age of a trout?
a: By the annual rings on its scales
By the colour of its eyes
By the length of its snout
9347.e: Rings form on the scales, similar to trees. In winter they grow more slowly, which you can see under a microscope.

9353.q: What do you measure with an ammeter?
9353.e: An ammeter is put into a circuit to measure how much current flows per second. The unit for this is the ampere.

9368.q: Why do children get milk teeth first and permanent teeth later?
a: The jaw grows and later needs bigger teeth
Permanent teeth only grow at night
Milk teeth are made of milk
9368.e: A child's jaw is too small for big teeth. When the jaw grows, stronger permanent teeth come through.
9368.m: Teeth grow along with your jaw.

9382.q: What is the World Economic Forum (WEF), held every year in Switzerland?
a: A meeting of political and business leaders in Davos
9382.e: Every January, important politicians, business leaders and experts from all over the world meet at the WEF in Davos. They discuss global economic and political issues.
9382.m: The WEF takes place every year in Davos.

9420.q: What does “change” mean when you pay?
a: The money you get back when paying
9420.e: If you pay with a larger note, you get the rest back as change. It is worth counting it.
9420.m: Change is what is left over when you pay.

9422.q: Which colourful bird dives for small fish, including young trout?
9422.e: The kingfisher sits on a branch by the water and plunges down onto its prey. Its feathers shimmer blue and orange.

9423.q: What is the galaxy that our solar system belongs to called?
9423.e: The Milky Way is a huge galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars, including our sun. On clear nights you can see it as a bright band across the sky.
9423.m: Our solar system lies in the Milky Way.

9452.q: What can develop if red blood cells do not get enough iron?
9452.e: Without enough iron, red blood cells can carry less oxygen. This is called anaemia and makes you tired and pale.
9452.m: A lack of iron can cause anaemia.

9457.q: What is the difference between coins and banknotes?
a: Coins are made of metal and usually worth less, notes are made of a special material and meant for larger amounts
Coins are always worth more than notes
9457.e: Coins are made of metal and usually have smaller values. Notes are made of a special material and are meant for larger amounts. In Switzerland there are coins from 5 rappen to 5 francs.
9457.m: Coins have small values, notes large ones.

9465.q: What happens at a book burning?
a: Books with unwanted ideas are burned.
Books are taken to a museum.
9465.e: In some dictatorships books the government did not like were burned in public. The aim was to make unwanted ideas disappear.

a: An organisation that supports poor countries with development projects
9485.e: The World Bank gives loans and know-how to countries so that they can build schools, roads or hospitals, for example. It works closely with the UN.
9485.m: The World Bank supports poorer countries financially.

9499.q: Who is the head of the Roman Catholic Church?
9499.e: The Pope lives in the Vatican in Rome and is the most important representative of the Catholic Church worldwide. He is elected by the cardinals.
9499.m: The Pope leads the Catholic Church.

9503.q: Some river power stations have a fish ladder made of many small pools. What is it for?
a: Fish can use it to get past weirs
Fish spend the winter in it
It keeps birds of prey away
9503.e: A fish ladder consists of small steps with pools. This lets fish swim upstream past weirs and dams.
9503.m: Fish ladders help fish over obstacles.

9527.q: Which sounds do African wild dogs use to communicate, among others?
9527.e: Wild dogs twitter and squeak to communicate. They also use body language.
9527.m: Wild dogs communicate with squeaks and calls.

9528.q: What are a plant’s leaves especially important for?
a: They hold the plant in the ground
9528.e: In the leaves the plant makes its own food with the help of sunlight, water and air. This happens mainly in the green leaves.

a: A slip on which you tick Yes or No
A letter from the Federal Council
9532.e: On the ballot paper you tick what you think about a question. This way you can help decide in a vote.

9574.q: Which endangered animal lives in the wild only in China and eats almost nothing but bamboo?
9574.e: The giant panda lives in the mountain forests of China and feeds almost entirely on bamboo. Thanks to conservation programmes, its numbers have recently recovered slightly.
9574.m: Pandas live in the wild only in China.

9576.q: What protects your brain from knocks?
9576.e: The skull is a hard bone that surrounds your brain like a helmet. That way it is well protected.
9576.m: The skull is the brain's helmet.

9581.q: Who forecasts on television whether it will rain or be sunny tomorrow?
9581.e: Meteorologists collect weather data and use it to make forecasts. That is how we find out what the weather will be like tomorrow.

9593.q: What is the planet Saturn especially known for?
a: Its striking ring system of ice and rock
Its solid surface you can walk on
9593.e: Saturn has wide, clearly visible rings made of countless small pieces of ice and rock. They make it especially easy to recognise through a telescope.
9593.m: Saturn has a large, clearly visible ring system.

a: A large community of living things with a typical climate, plants and animals
A single tree in a forest
9601.e: Biomes are large habitats such as tundra, steppe or rainforest, shaped by a characteristic climate and typical plants and animals. They occur in similar forms on different continents.
9601.m: Biomes are large habitats typical of a climate.

a: Steady winds near the equator that blow from high to low air pressure
Winds that only occur in the Alps
Winds that only blow in winter
9602.e: Trade winds are very regular winds that blow near the equator. In the past they were important for sailing ships.
9602.m: Trade winds blow regularly towards the equator.

9618.q: In the picture a trout is hiding. Where does it like to stay?
a: Under stones, roots and overhanging banks
On dry land on the bank
In the middle of a bare concrete slab
9618.e: Such hiding places protect it from enemies and from the strong current. It also lies in wait for prey from there.
9618.m: It hides under stones and roots.

9623.q: What does a magnifying glass do to the sun's rays?
a: It focuses them on one point
It turns them into heat without light
9623.e: A magnifying glass is curved and bends the light rays so that they meet at one point. It can get so hot there that paper starts to burn.
9623.m: A magnifying glass focuses light on one point.

9636.q: How can you vote without going to the ballot box in person?
a: With a show of hands in the classroom
9636.e: Many people in Switzerland vote by post. They send in their ballot paper by mail.

9658.q: Trout have a small extra fin without bony rays on their back, just before the tail fin. What is it called?
9658.e: Fish of the salmon family such as the brown trout have a small adipose fin in addition to the dorsal fin. It has no bony rays.
9658.m: Salmon-family fish have a small adipose fin.

9679.q: What is the minimum age to be elected to the National Council?
9679.e: In Switzerland, anyone who is allowed to vote may also stand for election to the National Council. So the minimum age is 18.
9679.m: From 18 you can stand as a candidate.

9692.q: What do you get when a cloud reaches right down to the ground?
9692.e: Fog is made of tiny water droplets floating in the air. It is really a cloud lying on the ground.
9692.m: Fog is a cloud on the ground.

12870.q: What did the Earth form from?
12870.e: Dust and lumps of rock were circling in space. They crashed into each other and stuck together into bigger and bigger lumps until the Earth was formed.
12870.m: The Earth formed from dust and rock circling in space.

12871.e: The Sun formed first. Then the planets, including the Earth, formed from what was left around the Sun.
12871.m: The Sun is older than the Earth.

12872.q: What was the Earth like at the very beginning?
12872.e: The young Earth was so hot that its rock glowed and was liquid. Only slowly did it cool down.
12872.m: The young Earth was glowing hot.

12873.e: Lava is rock that is so hot it becomes liquid. It comes out of the Earth at volcanoes.
12873.m: Lava is liquid, glowing hot rock.

12874.q: According to scientists today, how was the Moon formed?
12874.e: Scientists think that a large body in space crashed into the young Earth. The Moon formed from the debris.
12874.m: The Moon probably formed after a big collision with the Earth.

12875.q: Where did the first life on Earth appear?
12875.e: Scientists think that the first living things appeared in water. The water probably protected them from the Sun’s dangerous rays.
12875.m: The first life probably appeared in water.

12876.q: How big were the first living things?
12876.e: The first living things were so small that you can only see them with a microscope. They were single-celled organisms like bacteria.
12876.m: The first living things were tiny single-celled organisms.

12877.q: Which planet is the Earth, counting from the Sun?
12877.e: From the Sun, first come Mercury and Venus, then the Earth. That is why the Earth is the third planet.
12877.m: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun.

12878.e: The Earth is almost as round as a ball. You can see this clearly on photos taken from space.
12878.m: The Earth is almost the shape of a ball.

12879.q: What was there a lot of on the young Earth?
12879.e: On the young Earth volcanoes erupted everywhere. There were no plants or animals yet.
12879.m: There were very many volcanoes on the young Earth.

12880.q: What formed when the Earth slowly cooled down and it rained for a long time?
12880.e: When the Earth cooled down, water vapour turned into rain. The water collected in the low places and formed the seas.
12880.m: When the Earth cooled down, the seas formed.

12881.q: What is it like deep inside the Earth?
12881.e: Inside the Earth it is still very hot today. The deeper you go, the hotter it gets.
12881.m: Inside the Earth it is very hot.

12882.q: What is the centre of the Earth called?
12882.e: Right in the middle of the Earth is the core. It is made mainly of iron.
12882.m: The centre of the Earth is called the core.

12883.q: What is the outermost, solid layer of the Earth that we live on called?
12883.e: The Earth’s crust is the outer, solid layer of the Earth. Compared with the whole Earth it is as thin as the skin of an apple.
12883.m: We live on the Earth’s crust.

12884.q: Who lived on Earth first: fish or dinosaurs?
12884.e: Fish existed long before the dinosaurs. The dinosaurs came much later.
12884.m: Fish existed long before the dinosaurs.

12885.q: Do the continents always stay in the same place?
a: Yes, they are tied to the seabed.
12885.e: The continents move only a few centimetres each year. But over millions of years they travel a long way.
12885.m: The continents move very slowly across the Earth.

12886.q: What was the name of the huge continent at the time of the first dinosaurs, in which almost all land was joined together?
12886.e: More than 200 million years ago, when the first dinosaurs lived, almost all the land on Earth was joined together. This giant continent is called Pangaea.
12886.m: The giant continent Pangaea later broke up into today’s continents.

12887.e: Africa slowly pushed against Europe. The rock was squeezed together and folded upwards, and that is how the Alps were formed.
12887.m: The Alps were formed because rock was pushed together.

12888.q: What do people sometimes find high up in the Swiss Alps?
12888.e: The rock of the Alps used to lie on the seabed. That is why fossilised shells and snails are found up there.
12888.m: Fossilised sea creatures are found in the Alps.

12889.e: The word comes from Greek. “Deinos” means terrible and “sauros” means lizard.

a: They were born alive like calves.
They grew in their mother’s pouch.
12890.e: Dinosaurs laid eggs, just as birds and crocodiles do today. Scientists have found many fossilised dinosaur eggs.

12891.e: Tyrannosaurus rex was a big meat-eater. It had a huge mouth with sharp teeth.

12892.q: What was strikingly small on Tyrannosaurus rex?
12892.e: Tyrannosaurus rex had a huge head and strong legs. But its arms were very short.
12892.m: Tyrannosaurus rex had very short arms.

12893.q: On how many legs did Tyrannosaurus rex walk?
12893.e: Tyrannosaurus rex walked on its two powerful back legs. It kept its balance with its long tail.
12893.m: Tyrannosaurus rex walked on two legs.

12894.q: How many horns did Triceratops have on its face?
12894.e: “Triceratops” means three-horned face. It had two long horns above its eyes and a short one on its nose.
12894.m: Triceratops had three horns on its face.

12895.e: Triceratops was a plant-eater. It used its beak to pluck plants.

12896.q: What was especially long on Brachiosaurus?
12896.e: Brachiosaurus had a very long neck. This let it eat leaves high up in the trees.
12896.m: Brachiosaurus had a very long neck.

12897.q: What did Stegosaurus have on its back?
12897.e: Stegosaurus had a row of large bony plates on its back. On its tail it had sharp spikes.
12897.m: Stegosaurus had large plates on its back.

12898.q: What did Ankylosaurus have at the end of its tail?
12898.e: Ankylosaurus had armour made of bony plates. At the end of its tail it had a heavy club of bone that it could use to defend itself.
12898.m: Ankylosaurus had a bony club on its tail.

12899.q: What did some dinosaurs, for example Velociraptor, have?
12899.e: Scientists have found out that many smaller dinosaurs had feathers. Velociraptor was one of them.

12900.q: Which animals today are descended from dinosaurs?
12900.e: Birds developed from small, feathered dinosaurs. You could say that birds are today’s dinosaurs.

12901.q: What do we call scientists who study dinosaur fossils?
12901.e: Palaeontologists study living things from prehistoric times. They dig up fossils and examine them.

12902.q: How do we know what dinosaurs looked like?
12902.e: Nobody has ever seen a dinosaur. Scientists put fossilised bones together and so find out how the animals were built.
12902.m: Fossilised bones show us what dinosaurs looked like.

12903.q: Did humans and dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus rex live at the same time?
12903.e: Many millions of years lie between the big dinosaurs and the first humans. Films in which people fight dinosaurs are made up.
12903.m: Humans and big dinosaurs never lived at the same time.

12904.q: Which period of Earth’s history is named after the Jura mountains?
12904.e: The Jurassic is a period when many dinosaurs lived. It is named after the Jura mountains, where rock from this time was studied.
12904.m: The Jurassic period is named after the Jura mountains.

12905.q: Which dinosaur has often been found in Frick in the canton of Aargau?
12905.e: Many Plateosaurus skeletons were found in a clay pit in Frick. You can see them in the dinosaur museum in Frick.
12905.m: Many Plateosaurus were found in Frick in Aargau.

12906.q: What can you see near Lommiswil in the canton of Solothurn?
12906.e: In an old quarry near Lommiswil you can see many dinosaur footprints on a large slab of rock. They are about 145 million years old.
12906.m: There are dinosaur footprints near Lommiswil.

a: No, some were as small as a chicken.
Yes, all were bigger than a house.
Yes, all were bigger than an elephant.
No, all were as tiny as ants.
12907.e: There were huge dinosaurs, but small ones too. Some were only as big as a chicken.

12908.q: Roughly how many years ago did the dinosaurs die out?
12908.e: That is so long ago that it is hard to imagine. At that time the age of the big dinosaurs came to an end.
12908.m: The dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.

12909.q: What hit the Earth shortly before the dinosaurs died out?
12909.e: A huge asteroid crashed into the Earth. That was the main reason the dinosaurs died out.
12909.m: A huge asteroid hit the Earth.

a: A lump of rock in space
A small moon of the Earth
12910.e: Asteroids are lumps of rock or metal that circle the Sun. Some are small, others are many kilometres across.
12910.m: An asteroid is a lump of rock in space.

12911.q: Roughly how big was the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs?
a: About as big as a car
About as big as a football
12911.e: The asteroid was about 10 to 15 kilometres across. That is more than the height of the highest mountain on Earth.
12911.m: The asteroid was many kilometres across.

12912.q: In which present-day country is the asteroid’s crater?
12912.e: The crater is on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. It is called the Chicxulub crater and is covered over today.
12912.m: The asteroid’s crater is in Mexico.

12913.q: What happened to the sky after the impact?
a: There were never any clouds again.
12913.e: The impact threw huge amounts of dust and soot into the air. They darkened the sky for a long time.
12913.m: After the impact, dust darkened the sky.

12914.q: Why did it become cold on Earth after the impact?
a: Sunlight could no longer get through.
12914.e: The dust in the air blocked the sunlight. That is why it became dark and cold all over the Earth for a long time.
12914.m: Without sunlight it became cold on Earth.

12915.q: Roughly how many kinds of animals and plants died out at that time?
a: About three out of four kinds
About one out of a hundred kinds
12915.e: Scientists estimate that about three quarters of all kinds of animals and plants died out at that time. It was one of the biggest mass extinctions in Earth’s history.
12915.m: About three out of four kinds died out at that time.

12916.q: Why did the big plant-eaters also have problems afterwards?
12916.e: Because many plants died, the big plant-eaters could no longer find enough to eat. After that the meat-eaters had no prey either.
12916.m: Without plants the plant-eaters had no food.

12917.q: Apart from the asteroid, what probably also had an effect?
a: Huge forest fires started by people
12917.e: At about the same time huge volcanoes erupted in India. They also changed the climate on Earth.
12917.m: Huge volcanic eruptions also made life hard for the animals.

12918.q: Which animals survived when the dinosaurs died out?
12918.e: Small mammals needed little food and could hide. So many of them survived.
12918.m: Small mammals survived the extinction of the dinosaurs.

12919.q: Which group of animals survived the extinction and still lives today?
12919.e: Crocodiles already existed at the time of the dinosaurs. Some smaller crocodiles survived the great extinction.
12919.m: Crocodiles survived the extinction of the dinosaurs.

12920.q: Which plants were the first to spread again in many places after the impact?
12920.e: Ferns were able to spread again quickly after the disaster. In some places scientists find especially many fern spores in rock layers from this time.
12920.m: After the impact, ferns were the first to spread.

12921.q: With which period of Earth’s history did the age of the big dinosaurs end?
12921.e: The last big dinosaurs lived in the Cretaceous period. At the end of the Cretaceous they died out, long before there were humans.
12921.m: The age of the big dinosaurs ended with the Cretaceous.

12922.q: Which sea creatures with coiled shells died out together with the dinosaurs?
12922.e: Ammonites were sea creatures with a coiled shell, related to squid. They died out in the same great extinction as the dinosaurs.
12922.m: Ammonites died out together with the dinosaurs.

12923.q: Did the dinosaurs die out in a single day?
12923.e: Many animals died right at the impact. Others only died later, because the cold and hunger lasted a long time.
12923.m: The dinosaurs took longer than one day to die out.

12924.q: What formed when the asteroid struck a sea?
12924.e: The asteroid crashed into a shallow sea. This created huge flood waves that rushed far over the coasts.
12924.m: The impact set off huge flood waves.

12925.q: Which big meat-eater was one of the last dinosaurs?
12925.e: Tyrannosaurus rex lived at the very end of the age of the dinosaurs. It died out in the great extinction.
12925.m: Tyrannosaurus rex was one of the last dinosaurs.

12926.q: How do scientists know that an asteroid struck at that time?
a: From stories told by early humans
12926.e: Scientists have found a thin layer of rock from that time all over the world. It contains substances that come from space.
12926.m: Traces in the rock reveal the asteroid impact.

12927.q: Kinds of animals are dying out today too. Who is often to blame for this today?
12927.e: Today kinds of animals often die out because people destroy their habitats or hunt them too much. That is why protecting nature is important.
12927.m: Today kinds of animals often die out because of people.

12928.q: On which continent did the first humans live?
12928.e: The first humans lived in Africa. From there they later spread all over the world.
12928.m: The first humans lived in Africa.

12929.q: What could early humans do better than apes?
12929.e: Early humans walked upright on two legs. This left their hands free for tools.
12929.m: Early humans walked upright on two legs.

12930.q: What is the name of the famous skeleton of an early human female from Ethiopia?
12930.e: Lucy was found in Ethiopia in Africa. She lived more than 3 million years ago and already walked upright.
12930.m: Lucy is a famous skeleton from Africa.

12931.q: What did the first humans make their tools from?
12931.e: The first humans shaped stones so that they had sharp edges. They did not yet know about metal and glass.
12931.m: The first tools were made of stone.

12932.q: Why is the Stone Age called that?
a: Because tools were made of stone
Because all houses were made of stone
12932.e: In the Stone Age people made many tools and weapons from stone. They did not yet know about metal.
12932.m: The Stone Age is called that because the tools were made of stone.

12933.q: What is the name of a large stone tool that was held in one hand?
12933.e: The hand axe was a stone that was chipped sharp on both sides. It fitted well in the hand.
12933.m: The hand axe was an important Stone Age tool.

12934.q: Which stone was especially popular for sharp tools in the Stone Age?
12934.e: Flint is easy to split and gets very sharp edges. It is also called silex.
12934.m: Flint was especially popular for sharp tools.

12935.q: What gave early humans warmth and light at night?
12935.e: Early humans learned to use fire. It gave warmth and light, kept wild animals away and made food softer.
12935.m: Fire gave early humans warmth and light.

12936.q: How did the first humans get their food?
12936.e: The first humans were hunter-gatherers. They hunted animals and gathered berries, nuts, roots and mushrooms. Fields and farm animals only came much later.

12937.q: Where did early humans often live?
12937.e: Many early humans lived in caves or under rock overhangs. They also built tents from wood and animal skins.
12937.m: Early humans often lived in caves and tents.

12938.q: Why did early humans often move on?
a: They followed the animals and the food.
12938.e: Hunter-gatherers followed the herds of animals and looked for new plants. That is why they rarely stayed in the same place for long.

12939.q: What did Stone Age people make their clothes from?
12939.e: Stone Age people sewed their clothes from furs and leather. This kept them warm in winter.
12939.m: In the Stone Age people wore clothes made of fur.

12940.q: What did Stone Age people sew with?
12940.e: Stone Age people carved fine needles from bone. They did not yet know about metal.
12940.m: Stone Age people sewed with bone needles.

12941.q: What did Stone Age people paint on cave walls?
12941.e: Many cave paintings show animals such as horses, bison and deer. The pictures are many thousands of years old.
12941.m: Stone Age people painted animals on cave walls.

12942.q: In which country is the famous painted cave of Lascaux?
12942.e: The cave of Lascaux is in France. Its animal pictures are many thousands of years old.
12942.m: The painted cave of Lascaux is in France.

12943.q: Which animal was probably the first pet of humans?
12943.e: The dog is descended from the wolf. According to what we know today, it was the first animal to live together with people. One of the oldest dog finds comes from the Kesslerloch cave near Thayngen.
12943.m: The dog was probably the first pet of humans.

12944.q: What are the early humans called who lived in Europe before us?
12944.e: The Neanderthals lived in Europe for a long time, including during the Ice Age. They are named after the Neander Valley in Germany.
12944.m: The Neanderthals lived in Europe before us.

12945.q: What is the name of the human species that all people today belong to?
12945.e: All people today belong to the species Homo sapiens. This is Latin and means “wise human”.
12945.m: All people today belong to Homo sapiens.

12946.q: Which musical instrument did Stone Age people already make?
12946.e: Scientists have found flutes made of bird bones and mammoth ivory. The oldest are more than 40,000 years old.
12946.m: There were bone flutes even in the Stone Age.

12947.q: What did Stone Age people often hunt with?
12947.e: Stone Age hunters used spears with tips made of stone or bone. They often hunted together.
12947.m: Stone Age hunters hunted with spears.

12948.q: What was it like in the Ice Age?
12948.e: In the Ice Age it was much colder than today. Large parts of the Earth were covered with ice.
12948.m: In the Ice Age it was much colder than today.

12949.q: What covered large parts of Switzerland in the Ice Age?
12949.e: In the Ice Age the glaciers from the Alps grew far out into the Swiss Plateau. At the coldest times most of Switzerland lay under ice.
12949.m: In the Ice Age a large part of Switzerland lay under glaciers.

12950.q: Which animal with long fur and tusks lived in the Ice Age?
12950.e: The mammoth had long, curved tusks. Thick, long fur protected it from the cold.
12950.m: The mammoth had thick fur against the cold.

12951.q: Which animal today is the mammoth related to?
12951.e: The mammoth belongs to the elephant family. Like elephants, it had a trunk and tusks.
12951.m: The mammoth is related to the elephant.

12952.q: In which village in the canton of Zurich were many mammoth bones found?
12952.e: Bones of several mammoths were found in Niederweningen in the canton of Zurich. You can see the finds in the Mammoth Museum.
12952.m: Many mammoth bones were found in Niederweningen.

12953.q: Which rhinoceros lived in Europe in the Ice Age?
12953.e: The woolly rhinoceros had thick, shaggy fur. This let it live in the cold of the Ice Age.
12953.m: The woolly rhinoceros lived in Europe in the Ice Age.

12954.q: Which big bear from the Ice Age is extinct today?
12954.e: The cave bear was bigger than today’s brown bear and spent the winter resting in caves. Its bones have also been found in Swiss caves such as the Wildkirchli in the Alpstein.
12954.m: The cave bear lived in the Ice Age and is extinct today.

12955.q: Which cat with very long canine teeth lived in the Ice Age?
12955.e: The sabre-toothed cat had two very long upper canine teeth. It is extinct today.
12955.m: The sabre-toothed cat had very long canine teeth.

12956.q: Which animals that live in the far north today also lived in Switzerland in the Ice Age?
12956.e: In the cold Ice Age reindeer also lived in Switzerland. Today they live only in the far north.
12956.m: There were reindeer in Switzerland in the Ice Age.

a: A big stone carried along by a glacier
An animal frozen in the ice
A bird from the Ice Age
12957.e: Glaciers carried huge stones far away from their mountains. When the ice melted, they were left behind. They are called erratic boulders.
12957.m: An erratic boulder is a stone brought by a glacier.

12958.q: What helped to shape many Swiss lakes, for example Lake Zurich?
12958.e: The Ice Age glaciers carved out deep valleys. When the ice melted, they filled with water and became lakes.
12958.m: Many Swiss lakes were shaped by glaciers.

12960.q: Roughly how many years ago did the last ice age end?
12960.e: The last ice age came to an end about 12,000 years ago. After that it became warmer and the glaciers melted.
12960.m: The last ice age ended about 12,000 years ago.

12961.q: What happened when the Ice Age came to an end?
12961.e: At the end of the Ice Age it became warmer. The glaciers melted and retreated into the Alps.
12961.m: At the end of the Ice Age the glaciers melted.

12962.q: What was the sea level like in the Ice Age?
12962.e: In the Ice Age a lot of water was frozen in glaciers. That is why the sea level was lower than today.
12962.m: In the Ice Age the sea level was lower than today.

12963.q: Were there already people in the Ice Age?
a: Yes, they hunted wild horses, for example.
12963.e: People lived long before the end of the Ice Age. They hunted wild horses and bison, for example.
12963.m: There were already people in the Ice Age.

12964.q: What is the name of the largest glacier in the Alps?
12964.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais is the largest and longest glacier in the Alps. But in the Ice Age the glaciers were much bigger still.
12964.m: The Great Aletsch Glacier is the largest glacier in the Alps.

12965.q: Which large animal did people in the Ice Age sometimes hunt together?
12965.e: A mammoth was too big for a single hunter. That is why people sometimes hunted it in groups.
12965.m: In the Ice Age, people sometimes hunted mammoths.

12966.q: What did Ice Age people use from a mammoth?
12966.e: People used almost everything from a mammoth: meat for eating, fur for clothes and bones for tools.
12966.m: People used the meat, fur and bones of the mammoth.

12967.q: Which tool did not exist yet in the Stone Age?
12967.e: People in the Stone Age did not yet know about iron. Tools were made of stone, wood and bone.
12967.m: There were no iron tools in the Stone Age.

12968.q: Which age followed the Stone Age in Europe?
12968.e: After the Stone Age, people learned how to make bronze. That is why the next great age is called the Bronze Age.
12968.m: The Bronze Age followed the Stone Age.

12969.q: What is the oldest part of the Stone Age called?
12969.e: The Old Stone Age is the oldest and longest part of the Stone Age. It lasted much longer than all the later parts put together.
12969.m: The Old Stone Age is the oldest part of the Stone Age.

12970.q: What is the last part of the Stone Age called?
12970.e: The New Stone Age is the most recent part of the Stone Age. After it came the age of metals.
12970.m: The New Stone Age is the last part of the Stone Age.

12971.q: Roughly how long did the Stone Age last?
12971.e: The oldest stone tools are more than two million years old. This makes the Stone Age the longest period in human history.
12971.m: The Stone Age is the longest period in human history.

12972.q: What did NOT exist yet in the Stone Age?
12972.e: Stone Age people in Europe could not write yet. That is why much of what we know about them comes only from finds in the ground.
12972.m: Stone Age people could not write yet.

12973.q: Who searches the ground for traces from the Stone Age?
12973.e: Archaeologists dig carefully in the ground. They find tools, bones and the remains of houses.
12973.m: Archaeologists find traces of the Stone Age in the ground.

12974.q: What is the name of the famous glacier mummy found in the Alps?
12974.e: Ötzi was found in 1991 in the ice of the Ötztal Alps. He lived around 5300 years ago, at the end of the Stone Age.
12974.m: Ötzi is a man from the Stone Age who was found in the ice.

12975.q: What was it like in the Ice Age, when many Stone Age people lived?
12975.e: In the Ice Age it was much colder than today. Huge glaciers also covered large parts of Switzerland.
12975.m: In the Ice Age, most of Switzerland was covered in ice.

12976.q: What did people gather in the Stone Age?
12976.e: People gathered berries, nuts, mushrooms, roots and herbs. This was an important part of their food.
12976.m: Hunter-gatherers also ate berries, nuts and mushrooms.

12978.q: What do we call people who do not live in one fixed place?
12978.e: Nomads move from place to place. Hunter-gatherers lived like this.
12978.m: Nomads do not always live in the same place.

12980.q: What did hunters use from an animal they had killed?
12980.e: They ate the meat and made clothes from the fur. They made tools from bones and antlers.
12980.m: Hunters used almost everything from an animal.

12981.q: Which animal did people often hunt in the Ice Age?
12981.e: In the Ice Age, large herds of reindeer lived in our region. They were very important for hunters.
12981.m: In the Ice Age, people often hunted reindeer.

12982.e: Hunter-gatherers lived in small groups, often with their family. Together they could hunt better and protect themselves.

12984.q: Why did people in the Stone Age use caves?
a: As a hiding place for gold
12984.e: Caves gave shelter from cold, rain and wind. People often lived at the entrance of the cave.
12984.m: Caves gave people shelter from the weather and the cold.

12985.q: Where else did Stone Age people often live when there was no cave?
12985.e: Many Stone Age people lived in tents made of animal skins and poles. Not everyone lived in caves.
12985.m: Many Stone Age people lived in tents made of skins.

12988.q: Which early humans are named after a valley in Germany?
12988.e: The Neanderthals are named after the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf. Their bones were found there.
12988.m: The Neanderthals are named after a valley in Germany.

12989.q: Which large Ice Age animal hibernated in caves?
12989.e: The cave bear was much bigger than a brown bear today and ate mainly plants. In winter it slept in caves, where many of its bones have been found.
12989.m: The cave bear spent the winter in caves.

12990.q: Where did Stone Age people sleep?
12990.e: People put furs, grass or leaves on the ground. They slept on them, often close to the fire.
12990.m: Stone Age people slept on furs on the ground.

12991.q: What did Stone Age people like to wear as jewellery?
12991.e: People made necklaces from shells, animal teeth and stones. They did not know about metal or glass yet.
12991.m: Jewellery made of shells and animal teeth existed even in the Stone Age.

12992.q: Which famous cave in Switzerland is near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen?
12992.e: In the Kesslerloch near Thayngen, many tools, pieces of jewellery and animal bones from the Ice Age were found. It is one of the most important sites in Switzerland.
12992.m: The Kesslerloch near Thayngen is a famous Ice Age site.

12993.q: Which animal is shown in the famous engraving from the Kesslerloch?
12993.e: In the Kesslerloch, a piece of reindeer antler with an engraved reindeer was found. Today it is called the “Searching Reindeer”; it used to be called the “Grazing Reindeer”.
12993.m: An engraved reindeer was found in the Kesslerloch.

12994.q: What did Stone Age people need fire for?
12994.e: Fire gave warmth and light. People could also roast meat with it.
12994.m: Fire gave people warmth, light and cooked food.

12995.q: Which animals did fire keep away?
12995.e: Many wild animals are afraid of fire. So people were better protected at night.
12995.m: Fire protected people from wild animals.

12996.q: How could Stone Age people make fire?
12996.e: People struck a flint against a stone such as pyrite. The sparks fell onto dry material.
12996.m: You could strike sparks for a fire with stones.

12997.q: How can you make fire without stones?
12997.e: If you spin a wooden stick quickly on a board, the wood gets hot. This makes a small glowing ember.
12997.m: Rubbing wood quickly can make an ember.

12998.q: What is the dry material that catches the sparks first called?
12998.e: Tinder catches sparks easily and starts to glow. People used, for example, a dried tree fungus.
12998.m: Tinder catches sparks and starts to glow.

12999.q: Where did the first humans probably get their first fire from?
12999.e: Lightning could set a tree on fire. The first humans took fire from such fires and looked after it carefully.
12999.m: The first humans probably took fire from fires caused by lightning.

13000.q: What was placed around a fireplace?
13000.e: Stones around the fire kept it together. Archaeologists often recognise old fireplaces by such stones and ash.
13000.m: Fireplaces were often ringed with stones.

13001.q: What is left in the ground from an old fire?
13001.e: Burnt wood turns into charcoal and ash. This shows archaeologists where a fire once burned.
13001.m: Charcoal and ash show where a fire burned.

13002.e: Cooked or roasted meat is softer. It is easier to chew and to digest.
13002.m: Roasted meat is softer and easier to eat.

13003.q: Which stone was especially popular for tools?
13003.e: Flint breaks into sharp pieces. It was good for cutting and scraping.

13004.q: What is a large stone tool that you hold in your fist called?
13004.e: The hand axe is one of the oldest human tools. People held it in their hand and probably used it for cutting and chopping.
13004.m: The hand axe is a very old stone tool.

13005.q: What was a stone blade used for?
13005.e: People cut meat and skins with sharp stone blades. They were the knives of the Stone Age.
13005.m: Stone blades were the knives of the Stone Age.

13006.q: What was at the front of a Stone Age arrow?
13006.e: The arrows had tips made of flint or bone. Metal was not known yet.
13006.m: Stone Age arrows had stone tips.

13007.q: Apart from stone, what else did people make tools from?
13007.e: Animal bones and antlers were hard and easy to shape. People made many tools and hunting weapons from them.
13007.m: Bone and antler were also important materials.

13009.q: What did people do with a harpoon made of bone?
13009.e: A harpoon has barbs. With it, people could spear fish and hold on to them.

13010.q: Which hunting weapon did people invent in the Stone Age to shoot from far away?
13010.e: With a bow and arrow, people could hit animals from a distance. The crossbow, catapult and cannon came much later.
13010.m: The bow and arrow have existed since the Stone Age.

13011.q: How did a flint get a sharp edge?
a: It was thrown into the grass
13011.e: People knocked pieces off with another stone or a piece of antler. This made a sharp edge.
13011.m: Knocking pieces off made a flint sharp.

13013.q: In which country is the Cave of Altamira?
13013.e: The Cave of Altamira is in the north of Spain. Large pictures of bison can be seen there.
13013.m: Bison are painted in the Cave of Altamira in Spain.

13015.q: What did Stone Age people make their paints from?
13015.e: Red and yellow paint came from coloured earth called ochre. Black was made from charcoal.
13015.m: Stone Age paints were made from earth and charcoal.

13016.q: Which part of the body did people often print on the wall?
13016.e: Handprints are found in many caves. Sometimes people put their hand on the wall and blew paint around it.
13016.m: Stone Age handprints are often found in caves.

13019.q: What protected the woolly mammoth from the cold?
13019.e: The woolly mammoth had long, thick fur. Underneath was a thick layer of fat.
13019.m: The woolly mammoth had thick fur against the cold.

13020.q: What are the long curved teeth of a mammoth called?
13020.e: Mammoths had very long, curved tusks. They probably used them to push snow away in winter to get to food.

13021.e: Mammoths were plant eaters. They ate mainly grass and herbs.

13022.q: Are there still living mammoths today?
13022.e: Mammoths died out a long time ago. We only know them from bones, finds and pictures.

13023.q: Where have whole mammoths been found lying in frozen ground?
13023.e: In Siberia the ground is frozen all year round. That is why some mammoths there were preserved with their skin and fur.
13023.m: Well-preserved mammoths have been found in the frozen ground of Siberia.

13024.q: Which village in the canton of Zurich has a mammoth museum?
13024.e: Mammoth bones were found in Niederweningen in the canton of Zurich. Today a museum there shows these finds.
13024.m: There is a mammoth museum in Niederweningen.

13025.q: Roughly how big was a woolly mammoth?
a: About as big as an elephant
About as big as a horse
About as big as a dog
About as big as a house
13025.e: A woolly mammoth was about 3 metres tall, roughly like an elephant today. It was not much bigger than many people think.
13025.m: A woolly mammoth was about as big as an elephant.

13026.q: Which animal living today was the mammoth related to?
13026.e: The mammoth belonged to the elephant family. Like elephants, it had a trunk and tusks.
13026.m: The mammoth was related to the elephant.

13027.q: What is the material of mammoth tusks called?
13027.e: Tusks are made of ivory. Stone Age people carved small figures and jewellery from it.
13027.m: People carved figures from mammoth ivory.

13028.q: What does it mean when people “settle down”?
13028.e: Settled people stay in the same place for a long time. They build permanent houses there.
13028.m: Settled people live permanently in one place.

13029.q: Why did the first farmers have to stay in the same place for a long time?
a: They had to look after their fields
They were not allowed to move away
13029.e: Fields need looking after, and you have to wait for the harvest. That is why farmers stayed near their fields.
13029.m: Farmers stayed near their fields until they could harvest.

13030.q: In which part of the Stone Age did people settle down?
13030.e: In the New Stone Age, people began to plant fields and keep animals. They stayed in one place while doing so.
13030.m: People settled down in the New Stone Age.

13031.q: Where did people first start farming crops?
13031.e: Farming began more than 10,000 years ago in the Middle East, in the so-called Fertile Crescent. From there it later spread to Europe too.
13031.m: Farming began in the Middle East.

13032.q: What did settled people build instead of tents?
13032.e: If you stay in one place, you build sturdy houses. Such houses lasted for many years.

13033.q: What could settled people do better than nomads?
13033.e: In permanent houses, people could store grain and other supplies. That way they also had food in winter.
13033.m: Settled people could store supplies for the winter.

13034.q: What do we call keeping and breeding animals?
13034.e: In livestock farming, people keep animals such as sheep or cattle. So they no longer had to rely only on hunting.
13034.m: In livestock farming, people keep their own animals.

13035.q: What do we call growing plants in fields?
13035.e: In arable farming, people sow seeds in fields and harvest later. This was a big new development of the New Stone Age.
13035.m: In arable farming, people sow and harvest in fields.

13036.q: What happened to the number of people when they settled down?
13036.e: With fields, animals and supplies, more people could be fed. That is why there were soon many more people than before.
13036.m: When people settled down, there were soon more people.

13037.q: Which grain did the first farmers grow?
13037.e: The first farmers in Europe mainly grew wheat and barley. Maize and potatoes came from America much later.
13037.m: The first farmers planted wheat and barley.

13038.q: Which animals did the first farmers keep?
13038.e: The first farmers kept sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. These animals gave meat, milk, wool and leather.
13038.m: The first farmers kept sheep, goats, cattle and pigs.

13039.q: How did the first farmers turn grains into flour?
a: They boiled them for a long time
They dried them in the sun
They chopped them with an axe
13039.e: The grains were ground on a flat stone with a smaller stone. A stone like this is called a millstone or quern.
13039.m: Farmers made flour with grinding stones.

13040.q: What did the first farmers make pots from?
13040.e: The farmers shaped pots from clay and fired them in the fire. They did not know about metals yet.
13040.m: The first farmers made pots from fired clay.

13041.q: Which plant did the first farmers make cloth from?
13041.e: People made threads from the fibres of flax. The cloth made from it is called linen.
13041.m: Linen cloth was made from flax.

13042.q: What did the first farmers use to cut grain?
13042.e: The first sickles had blades made of flint. They were used to cut the stalks.
13042.m: Grain was cut with a sickle.

13043.q: What did farmers do to make room for fields?
13043.e: At that time, much of the land was covered in forest. Farmers cut down trees to make fields.
13043.m: Farmers cleared forest for their fields.

13044.q: What did goats and cows give the farmers?
13044.e: Goats, sheep and cows gave milk. People probably already made cheese from it back then.
13044.m: Goats and cows gave the farmers milk.

13045.q: Apart from meat, what did sheep give the farmers?
13045.e: Sheep's wool could be spun into thread. Warm cloth was made from it.
13045.m: Sheep give wool for warm clothes.

13046.q: What was formed when several farming families lived close together?
13046.e: The first farmers built their houses close together. This is how the first villages were formed.
13046.m: The first villages were formed in the New Stone Age.

13047.q: What did the first farmers in Central Europe build their houses from?
13047.e: The frame was made of wooden posts. The walls were woven branches covered with clay.
13047.m: The first farmhouses were made of wood and clay.

13048.q: What did the first farmers cover their roofs with?
13048.e: Reeds and straw kept the rain out. But these roofs had to be repaired again and again.
13048.m: The roofs were covered with reeds or straw.

13049.q: What was sometimes built around a village for protection?
13049.e: Some villages had a fence of wooden stakes, called a palisade. It protected against wild animals and enemies.

13050.q: Why did the first farmers like to build their villages near water?
13050.e: Near water there was drinking water, and people could fish. Water was also important for the fields and animals.
13050.m: Villages were often near water because people needed it to live.

13051.q: What are the large houses of the first farmers in our region called?
13051.e: The first farmers built very long wooden houses, often 20 to 40 metres long. People lived in them and stored their supplies there.
13051.m: The first farmers lived in longhouses.

13052.q: What did many houses in the first villages have in the middle?
13052.e: The hearth fire burned in the middle or at one side. People cooked there, and it kept the house warm.
13052.m: A hearth fire burned in the houses.

13053.q: What did people in the New Stone Age make with a loom?
13053.e: With a loom, people wove threads into cloth. The oldest signs of looms come from the New Stone Age.
13053.m: Cloth was woven on a loom.

13054.q: What is the name of one of the oldest settlements in the world, in what is now Turkey?
13054.e: Çatalhöyük is one of the oldest known large settlements. The houses stood so close together that people walked across the roofs. Jericho is in the West Bank, Ur in Iraq and Mohenjo-Daro in Pakistan.
13054.m: Çatalhöyük in Turkey is a very old settlement.

13055.q: What did the houses of the lake dwellers stand on?
13055.e: The houses stood on wooden posts. This kept them dry, even when the water rose.
13055.m: Stilt houses stood on wooden posts.

13056.q: Where did the lake dwellers build their villages?
13056.e: The lake dwellers built their villages on the shores of lakes and in moors. Such villages existed in all the countries around the Alps.
13056.m: Lake dwellers lived on lake shores and in moors.

13057.q: Why have the wooden posts survived until today?
a: They lay in water and mud
They were freshly painted every year
13057.e: Under water and in mud there is no air. That is why the wood hardly rots there.
13057.m: The wood of the stilt houses was preserved in water and mud.

13058.q: What special heritage do the stilt houses around the Alps belong to?
a: The Seven Wonders of the World
13058.e: The stilt houses around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011. That is why they are specially protected.
13058.m: The stilt houses around the Alps are UNESCO World Heritage.

13059.q: Which country has the most World Heritage stilt house sites?
13059.e: Of the 111 World Heritage sites, 56 are in Switzerland. That is about half.
13059.m: About half of the World Heritage stilt house sites are in Switzerland.

13060.q: On which lake were remains of stilt houses found at Meilen?
13060.e: At Meilen on Lake Zurich, old posts and finds were discovered when the water level was very low. After that, people searched many lakes for stilt houses.
13060.m: Remains of stilt houses were found early on at Meilen on Lake Zurich.

13061.q: What, for example, did archaeologists find in stilt houses?
13061.e: In the stilt houses, people found pots, tools, cloth and even leftover food. So we know a lot about life back then.
13061.m: Finds from stilt houses show how people lived back then.

13062.q: What did the lake dwellers use to travel on the lake?
13062.e: A dugout canoe is a boat made from a single hollowed-out tree trunk. People used them to travel on the lakes and to fish.
13062.m: A dugout canoe is a boat made from a single tree trunk.

13063.q: What did the lake dwellers mainly live from?
13063.e: The lake dwellers were farmers. They had fields and animals, and they also fished and gathered food.
13063.m: The lake dwellers lived as farmers and fishers.

13064.q: On which continent was ancient Egypt?
13064.e: Egypt lies in the north-east of Africa. The kingdom of the pharaohs arose there about 5000 years ago.

13065.q: What is the capital of Egypt today?
13065.e: Cairo lies on the Nile and is Egypt's largest city. The Pyramids of Giza are close by.
13065.m: The capital of Egypt is Cairo.

13066.q: What kind of landscape covers most of Egypt?
13066.e: Almost all of Egypt is desert. Only along the Nile is there enough water for fields and villages.

13067.q: Which cereals did farmers in ancient Egypt mainly grow?
13067.e: The Egyptians mainly grew wheat and barley. They used the grain to bake bread, for example.
13067.m: Egyptian farmers mainly grew wheat and barley.

13068.q: Which drink did the ancient Egyptians make from barley?
13068.e: Beer was an everyday drink in ancient Egypt. It was brewed from barley and bread.
13068.m: The Egyptians brewed beer from barley.

13069.q: Which animal was especially loved and respected by the ancient Egyptians?
13069.e: Cats caught mice and snakes. They were even considered sacred animals of a goddess.
13069.m: The cat was highly respected in ancient Egypt.

13070.q: What did most Egyptians build their houses from?
13070.e: The houses were made of bricks of Nile mud, dried in the sun. Stone was mainly used for temples and tombs.
13070.m: Houses in Egypt were built of mud bricks.

13071.q: What fabric were the clothes of the ancient Egyptians usually made of?
13071.e: Linen is made from the flax plant. The light fabric was pleasant in the heat.
13071.m: The Egyptians usually wore light linen clothes.

13072.q: What was a popular board game of the ancient Egyptians called?
13072.e: Senet was played on a board with 30 squares. Senet games have even been found in tombs.
13072.m: The ancient Egyptians liked playing the board game Senet.

13073.q: Which animal often carried heavy loads in ancient Egypt?
13073.e: Donkeys were the most important pack animals. Camels only became common in Egypt much later.
13073.m: In ancient Egypt, donkeys carried heavy loads.

13074.q: Roughly how long did the kingdom of the pharaohs last?
13074.e: The kingdom of the pharaohs began about 5000 years ago. It only ended when the Romans conquered Egypt.
13074.m: The kingdom of the pharaohs lasted about 3000 years.

13075.q: What do you call researchers who dig old things out of the ground?
13075.e: Archaeologists carefully dig up tombs, houses and objects. This teaches us a lot about ancient Egypt.
13075.m: Archaeologists dig up and study old things.

13076.q: What is the great river that flows through Egypt called?
13076.e: The Nile flows from south to north through the whole of Egypt. Without it, hardly anyone could live there.
13076.m: The great river in Egypt is the Nile.

13077.q: What is true about the length of the Nile?
a: It is one of the longest rivers in the world
It is the shortest river in Africa
It is shorter than the Aare
It is only as long as a lake
13077.e: Depending on how it is measured, the Nile is over 6500 kilometres long. Together with the Amazon, it is one of the longest rivers on Earth.
13077.m: The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world.

13078.q: Into which sea does the Nile flow?
13078.e: The Nile flows into the Mediterranean in the north of Egypt. Before that, it splits into several branches.
13078.m: The Nile flows into the Mediterranean.

13079.q: What happened on the Nile every year in late summer in ancient Egypt?
13079.e: Heavy rains far to the south, in the highlands of Ethiopia, made the Nile swell every year. Then it flooded the fields along its banks.
13079.m: Every year the Nile flooded the fields.

13080.q: What did the Nile flood leave behind on the fields?
13080.e: The dark mud was a good fertiliser. Grain grew especially well on it.
13080.m: The flood brought fertile mud to the fields.

13081.q: The ancient Egyptians called their land ‘Kemet’. What does that mean?
13081.e: The name comes from the dark mud of the Nile. The desert, on the other hand, they called ‘red land’.
13081.m: Kemet means ‘black land’ because of the dark Nile mud.

13082.q: Which dangerous animal lived in the Nile?
13082.e: Many crocodiles lived in the Nile. People feared them and even worshipped a crocodile god.
13082.m: Dangerous crocodiles lived in the Nile.

13083.q: In German, which large animal has the river's name in its own name?
13083.e: In German the hippo is called ‘Nilpferd’, meaning ‘Nile horse’. Hippos live in rivers and lakes in Africa, and in ancient Egypt there were also hippos on the Nile.
13083.m: In German the hippo is named after the Nile.

13084.q: How did the ancient Egyptians move grain and large stones over long distances?
13084.e: The Nile was Egypt's most important road. Boats carried people, grain and even large stones from place to place.
13084.m: The Egyptians travelled by boat on the Nile.

13085.q: How did farmers bring Nile water to their fields?
13085.e: The farmers dug canals from the river to the fields. This way the plants had enough water even after the flood.
13085.m: Canals carried Nile water to the fields.

13086.q: Where did most people live in ancient Egypt?
a: On the banks of the Nile
In the middle of the desert
13086.e: Only along the Nile was there water and fertile soil. That is why almost all villages and towns were on the river.
13086.m: Most Egyptians lived on the banks of the Nile.

13087.q: What is the area called where the Nile splits into several branches before reaching the sea?
13087.e: The Nile Delta is shaped like a triangle. It looks like the Greek letter delta.
13087.m: Before the sea, the Nile splits into several branches in the delta.

13088.q: Which plant grew on the banks of the Nile and was very useful?
13088.e: Papyrus is a kind of reed. The Egyptians used it to make writing sheets, baskets, ropes and even boats.
13088.m: The useful papyrus plant grew along the Nile.

13090.q: What did the word ‘pharaoh’ originally mean?
13090.e: At first the word meant the royal palace. Later the king himself was called that.

13091.q: What did the ancient Egyptians believe about their pharaoh?
a: He is like a god on earth
He is a servant of the priests
He is a soldier like all the others
13091.e: The pharaoh was regarded as the son of the sun god. He was supposed to keep order in the land.
13091.m: The Egyptians saw the pharaoh as a god on earth.

13092.q: What did the pharaoh often wear on his head?
13092.e: The striped headcloth is called a nemes. You can also see it on the famous death mask of Tutankhamun.
13092.m: The pharaoh often wore a striped headcloth.

13093.q: What did the pharaoh wear on his chin at festivals?
13093.e: The false beard was a sign of royal dignity. It was fastened with straps.
13093.m: The pharaoh wore a false beard as a sign of his power.

13094.q: What did the pharaoh hold in his hands as a sign of his power?
13094.e: The crook is like a shepherd's staff. It shows that the pharaoh leads his people like a shepherd leads his flock.
13094.m: The crook and flail were signs of the pharaoh's power.

13095.q: Which animal sat on the front of the pharaoh's crown to protect him?
13095.e: The rearing cobra on the forehead was meant to frighten enemies away. It was a protective symbol of the king.
13095.m: A cobra on the crown protected the pharaoh.

13096.q: From how many parts was Egypt first united into one kingdom?
13096.e: There was Upper Egypt in the south and Lower Egypt in the north. That is why the pharaoh was also called ‘Lord of the Two Lands’.
13096.m: Egypt was formed from two parts, Upper and Lower Egypt.

13097.q: Which famous queen was the last to rule Egypt before the Romans conquered it?
13097.e: Cleopatra was the last queen of independent Egypt. When the Romans conquered Egypt, she died, and Egypt became part of the Roman Empire.
13097.m: Cleopatra was the last queen of ancient Egypt before the Romans.

13098.q: Which woman ruled as pharaoh herself and had a great terraced temple built near Luxor?
13098.e: Hatshepsut ruled as pharaoh for about 20 years. Her temple at Deir el-Bahari has three large terraces in front of a cliff.
13098.m: Hatshepsut was a woman who ruled as pharaoh herself.

13099.q: Which pharaoh ruled for a very long time and had the rock temples of Abu Simbel built?
13099.e: Ramesses II ruled for about 66 years. In front of his temple at Abu Simbel sit four giant statues of him.
13099.m: Ramesses II had the temples of Abu Simbel built.

13100.q: What is the valley where many pharaohs were buried in rock tombs called?
13100.e: The Valley of the Kings is near the city of Luxor. There the Egyptians dug deep tombs into the rock.
13100.m: Many pharaohs are buried in the Valley of the Kings.

13101.q: Which queen, the wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten, is famous for a painted bust?
13101.e: The colourful bust of Nefertiti is over 3000 years old. Today it is in a museum in Berlin.
13101.m: The bust of Queen Nefertiti is world-famous.

13102.q: What were the great pyramids built for?
13102.e: Pharaohs were buried in the pyramids. They were meant to secure their way into the afterlife.
13102.m: The pyramids were tombs for pharaohs.

13103.q: On which side of the Nile did the Egyptians build most pyramids and tombs?
a: In the west, where the sun sets
In the east, where the sun rises
On islands in the middle of the Nile
13103.e: The Egyptians linked the west, where the sun sets, with the realm of the dead. That is why most pyramids and tombs are on the west bank of the Nile.
13103.m: Most pyramids and tombs are west of the Nile.

13104.q: How many great pyramids stand side by side at Giza?
13104.e: They are the pyramids of the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure. There are also a few small pyramids next to them.
13104.m: There are three great pyramids at Giza.

13105.q: What shape is the base of an Egyptian pyramid?
13105.e: The base is square. The four sides are triangles that meet at a point at the top.
13105.m: A pyramid has a square base.

13106.q: What were the great pyramids built from?
13106.e: The Great Pyramid of Khufu needed over two million stone blocks. Many of them are heavier than a car.
13106.m: The pyramids are made of huge stone blocks.

13107.q: Roughly how tall is the Great Pyramid of Khufu (Cheops)?
13107.e: It used to be almost 147 metres tall; today it is about 139 metres. That is roughly as tall as a 45-storey tower block.
13107.m: The Great Pyramid of Khufu is about 140 metres tall.

13108.q: What is special about the Great Pyramid of Khufu among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World?
a: It is the only one still standing
13108.e: The other six wonders have been destroyed or have disappeared. Only the Great Pyramid of Khufu still exists.
13108.m: The Great Pyramid of Khufu is the only ancient wonder still standing.

13109.q: According to what we know today, who built the pyramids?
13109.e: Thousands of workers and craftsmen built the pyramids. They lived in villages nearby and were paid in food.
13109.m: Thousands of Egyptian workers built the pyramids.

13110.q: How did the workers move the heavy stone blocks?
13110.e: The stones were pulled on wooden sledges and carried on boats across the Nile. Many workers pulled on ropes together.
13110.m: The stones were pulled on wooden sledges.

13111.q: What did the pyramid of the pharaoh Djoser, one of the oldest pyramids, look like?
13111.e: The Pyramid of Djoser looks like a staircase with six steps. Pyramids with smooth sides were only built later.
13111.m: The Pyramid of Djoser is a step pyramid.

13112.q: What were the Pyramids of Giza once covered with on the outside?
13112.e: A layer of pale, smooth limestone made the pyramids shine in the sun. Later these stones were taken away for other buildings.
13112.m: The pyramids once gleamed with smooth white stones.

13113.e: The pharaoh's coffin stood in the burial chamber. Passages led there from outside.
13113.m: Inside a pyramid was the burial chamber.

13114.q: What does the Great Sphinx near the Pyramids of Giza look like?
a: A lion's body with a human head
A horse's body with a bird's head
A human body with a cat's head
A snake's body with a lion's head
13114.e: The Sphinx lies like a lion and has the face of a pharaoh. It was carved out of the rock.
13114.m: The Sphinx has a lion's body and a human head.

13115.e: The Egyptians dried the bodies of the dead. This way they lasted a very long time.
13115.m: A mummy is a dead person whose body has been preserved.

13116.q: Why did the ancient Egyptians turn the dead into mummies?
a: Because the tombs were too small
13116.e: The Egyptians believed that the soul still needed the body in the afterlife. So the body was not supposed to decay.
13116.m: Mummies were meant to give the dead a life after death.

13117.q: What was a mummy wrapped in?
13117.e: Many metres of linen strips were wound around the body. Small protective amulets were often placed between them.
13117.m: Mummies were wrapped in linen bandages.

13118.q: What was used to dry the body of a mummy?
13118.e: The salt is called natron and is found in Egypt. It drew the water out of the body.
13118.m: A salt was used to dry the body.

13119.q: Which organ did the Egyptians usually leave inside the mummy's body?
13119.e: The heart was seen as the seat of thought and feeling. It was weighed in the afterlife and so had to stay in the body.
13119.m: The heart stayed in the mummy because it was needed in the afterlife.

13120.q: What were the removed organs kept in?
13120.e: These jars are called canopic jars. Their lids often had the heads of protective gods.
13120.m: The organs went into special jars, the canopic jars.

13121.q: Roughly how long did it take to make a mummy?
13121.e: Drying the body alone took many weeks. After that the body was anointed and wrapped.

13122.q: What is a large stone coffin that a mummy was placed in called?
13122.e: A sarcophagus is a coffin made of stone. It often held further wooden coffins inside.
13122.m: A large stone coffin is called a sarcophagus.

13123.q: Which god with a jackal's head protected the dead and the mummies?
13123.e: Anubis was the god of embalming. He watched over the tombs and the dead.
13123.m: Anubis with the jackal's head protected the dead.

13124.q: Were animals also mummified in ancient Egypt?
13124.e: Over a million animal mummies have been found, for example cats, birds and crocodiles. Many were gifts to the gods.
13124.m: Animals such as cats were also mummified.

13125.q: What did the Egyptians place in the tomb with the dead?
13125.e: The dead were supposed to have everything they needed in the afterlife. So they were given many everyday things.
13125.m: The dead were given food, furniture and jewellery in their tombs.

13126.q: What is the collection of magic spells written on papyrus and given to the dead called?
13126.e: The Book of the Dead was meant to help the dead survive the dangers of the afterlife. It contained spells and pictures.
13126.m: The Book of the Dead helped the dead on their way into the afterlife.

13127.e: Hieroglyphs are signs that look like small pictures. The ancient Egyptians wrote with them.
13127.m: Hieroglyphs are the picture writing of the ancient Egyptians.

13128.e: The word comes from Greek. The Greeks saw the signs mainly on temples.

13129.q: Roughly how many different hieroglyph signs were there?
13129.e: For a long time the Egyptians used about 700 different signs. That is far more than the 26 letters of our alphabet.
13129.m: There were several hundred different hieroglyph signs.

13130.q: Who could read and write hieroglyphs in ancient Egypt?
13130.e: Only a few people could read and write. Scribes studied for many years and were highly respected.
13130.m: Scribes were important and respected people in ancient Egypt.

13131.q: What did Egyptian scribes use to write on papyrus?
13131.e: The writing brush was made from a plant stem. Black ink was made from soot.
13131.m: The scribes wrote with a brush and ink.

13132.q: Where can you still find many hieroglyphs today?
13132.e: The Egyptians carved and painted hieroglyphs on the walls of temples and tombs. Many are still well preserved today.
13132.m: Many hieroglyphs are on temples and in tombs.

13133.q: In which direction could hieroglyphs be written?
13133.e: Hieroglyphs could run from right to left, from left to right or from top to bottom. Human and animal figures face the beginning of the text.
13133.m: Hieroglyphs could be written in several directions.

13134.q: What is the oval frame in which a pharaoh's name is written called?
13134.e: The cartouche is a ring around the royal name. It was meant to protect the pharaoh's name.
